title: Georgia's Sirish Subash Wins Top Young Scientist Title for AI Pesticide Detector
excerpt: The 14-year-old Indian-origin ninth grader's handheld device PestiSCAND detects pesticide residues on produce with over 85% accuracy, earning him the 2024 3M Young Scientist Challenge's $25,000 grand prize.
body:
• Sirish Subash, a 14-year-old Indian-origin ninth grader from Snellville, Georgia, won the 2024 3M Young Scientist Challenge and the title of "America's Top Young Scientist" for PestiSCAND, a handheld AI-based pesticide detector.
  • The $25,000 grand-prize device uses spectrophotometry and a machine learning model to detect pesticide residues on fruits and vegetables without damaging the produce, recording over 85% accuracy in tests on spinach and tomatoes.
  • Subash beat nine other finalists in the final events at 3M's global headquarters in St. Paul, Minnesota, on October 14-15, 2024, developing his prototype over the summer with mentor Aditya Banerji, a senior research engineer at 3M.
  • Beyond the lab, Subash is an Asia Book of Records honoree as the youngest non-fiction author at age 10, runs the science YouTube channel SciKid Sirish, and plans to invest his winnings in college tuition.

A 14-year-old Indian-origin student from Georgia has earned national recognition for building a handheld artificial-intelligence device that detects pesticide residues on fruits and vegetables. Sirish Subash, a ninth grader at the Gwinnett School of Mathematics, Science, and Technology in Snellville, won the 2024 3M Young Scientist Challenge — the United States' premier middle-school science competition — with his invention PestiSCAND, earning the title of "America's Top Young Scientist" and a $25,000 cash prize.

Subash spent four months competing against nine other finalists before securing his victory during the final challenge events at 3M's global headquarters in St. Paul, Minnesota, on October 14 and 15. The finalists were judged on innovative thinking, application of STEM principles, research, presentation skills, and their ability to inspire others.

Context & Background

The idea behind PestiSCAND started at the family dinner table. Subash's parents insist that he wash produce before eating it, which set him wondering whether rinsing actually removes pesticide contamination. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration estimates that about 60 percent of all produce contains pesticide residues, and washing removes only part of the contamination. Lingering residues have been linked to serious health risks, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's disease, and some cancers.

PestiSCAND works non-destructively: it measures how various wavelengths of light reflect off the surface of fruits and vegetables — spectrophotometry — and feeds that data into a machine learning model that determines whether pesticides are present. The device pairs a sensor, power supply, display screen, and processor, and is designed to work with a companion app.

Impact & Analysis

In testing, PestiSCAND identified pesticide residues on spinach and tomatoes with accuracy exceeding 85 percent, meeting the project's goals for both effectiveness and speed. That performance matters because food safety tools that ordinary consumers can afford and understand barely exist. The invention points toward a future in which a quick scan at the grocery store or in the kitchen could tell a family whether an extra rinse — or a different purchase — is warranted.

"The main goal of PestiSCAND is to help people ensure that they aren't consuming pesticides so they can avoid any associated health risks."

— Sirish Subash, 3M Young Scientist Challenge winner

The competition's mentorship structure was central to the result. Each finalist worked one-on-one with a 3M scientist over the summer to turn an idea into a working prototype, and Subash was paired with Aditya Banerji, a senior research engineer at 3M's Corporate Research Process Laboratory. The second- and third-place winners each received $2,000.

Diaspora Angle

Subash's win continues a strong run for Indian-origin students in American STEM competitions. In the same 2024 final, fellow Indian-origin finalists Ankan Das, Aakash Manaswi, Prince Nallamothula, Ronita Shukla, and Rithvik Suren placed in the fourth-to-tenth ranks. His journey also reflects a distinctly diaspora arc: his interest in science dates to the first grade, he skipped fifth grade, and he nearly missed his shot at the competition because his family spent much of his sixth-grade year in India.

His profile extends beyond science. Subash authored two books — Carbon Block Puzzle, on climate change, and Biochemistry: The Fun Way!, an illustrated graphic novel — and set the Asia Book of Records as the youngest non-fiction author at age 10. He also runs a YouTube channel, SciKid Sirish, where he explains science topics and experiments.

What's Next

Subash has said he wants to attend the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and plans to invest his winnings in college tuition, while continuing to develop devices and resources for everyday health. The 3M Young Scientist Challenge has a track record of launching young inventors — past winners have given TED Talks, filed patents, founded nonprofits, and made the Forbes 30 Under 30 list — and PestiSCAND's non-destructive, low-cost approach gives it genuine commercialization potential in the consumer food-safety space.
